question: A 35-year-old man has a groin swelling that appears on coughing and disappears on lying down. On examination the swelling is controlled by pressure over the deep inguinal ring (mid-point of the inguinal ligament). This hernia is best classified as:

answers.text: Direct inguinal hernia — passes through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A direct hernia passes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach's triangle; it is NOT controlled by pressure over the deep ring.

answers.text: Indirect inguinal hernia — passes through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and traverses the inguinal canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An indirect hernia enters via the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and is controlled by finger pressure over that ring — the hallmark distinguishing it from a direct hernia.

answers.text: Femoral hernia — passes through the femoral canal below and lateral to the pubic tubercle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A femoral hernia presents as a swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, NOT in the inguinal canal, and is not controlled by pressure over the deep inguinal ring.

answers.text: Pantaloon hernia — simultaneous direct and indirect components straddling the inferior epigastric vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A pantaloon (compound) hernia has both components. The scenario describes a single swelling controlled by ring pressure — consistent with a pure indirect hernia.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: indirect hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring; direct hernias push through Hesselbach's triangle medially and are NOT controlled by ring pressure.
Well done. The deep-ring control test is the bedside key to differentiating indirect from direct inguinal hernias.
